newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan seeks to limit damage from PM bombshell.
newsitem.headline: Japan seeks to limit damage from PM bombshell.

text.p: Japan, seeking to limit potential damage after a remark by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto sent U.S. financial markets reeling, denied on Tuesday that Tokyo intended to sell off U.S. government bonds.
Analysts, however, said the provocative comment by the outspoken Hashimoto could haunt bilateral ties.

Hashimoto, responding to a question after a speech at Columbia University in New York on Monday, said Japan had in the past been tempted to sell its holdings of U.S. Treasury securities and boost its gold reserves, but had not done so.

"I hope the U.S. will engage in efforts and in cooperation to maintain exchange stability so we will not succumb to the temptation to sell off Treasury bills and switch our funds to gold," Hashimoto added.

The comment, taken by U.S. markets as a veiled threat by Hashimoto to sell off Japan's U.S. Treasury holdings, undermined the dollar in New York and ignited a sell-off in U.S. shares which sliced 192.25 points off the Dow Jones industrial average. The decline was second only to the 508-point drop when the market crashed on October 19, 1987.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said on Tuesday that Hashimoto's "real intention was not reported correctly" and that Japan had no intention of selling U.S. Treasuries.

"We have not tried to sell U.S. Treasuries and the ministry has not thought about it," Mitsuzuka, changing planes outside Tokyo on his way from Denver, Colorado, to Beijing, told reporters. "We have no such intention at present."
A senior ministry official also told reporters that U.S. Treasuries were an essential part of Japan's foreign reserves.
"U.S. Treasuries are a highly advantageous, secure and essential investment instrument for Japan's foreign currency reserves," the official said.

The remark by Hashimoto -- an outspoken politician who made a name with his tough stance as trade minister in bitter U.S.-Japan talks in 1995 -- appeared to reflect frustration over U.S. criticism of his tight fiscal stance and its repeated warnings against a resurgent Japanese trade surplus and over Washington's lukewarm welcome for Tokyo's deregulation plans.

"America is putting very strong pressure on Japan. At the political level Japan's stance is to put up with this, but in economic circles and in society, people are getting...fed up," said political commentator Minoru Morita.

Speaking after the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations' summit in Denver, Colorado, on Sunday, U.S. President Bill Clinton warned Japan it risked economic war if its trade surplus ballooned again and took direct aim at the fiscal tightening which Hashimoto has pledged to carry out.

Faced with U.S. criticism, Hashimoto's quick temper may have prompted his provocative remark. "When he feels that he has been challenged...he tends to fight back," said Takeshi Kiuchi, chief economist at LTCB Research Institute.

But Japan is unlikely to follow through on Hashimoto's veiled threat -- which he has reportedly made before -- not least because the probable impact would be to boost the yen against the dollar and hurt Japan's exports and its economy.

"We're talking new historic lows (for the dollar) if they started doing that," said Kenneth Landon, currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "I don't think that it reflects the intention of Japan to sell U.S. securities. It was mostly a sign of frustration with U.S. haggling over the trade issue."
The comment could, however, harm U.S.-Japan ties by undermining mutual confidence. "I think Hashimoto misspoke and that it was not intentional," Morita said.

"The U.S. side has misgivings that Japan might sell its U.S. Treasuries and that concern will be strengthened. The U.S. will feel it cannot regard Japan as a completely faithful partner. This happening will have a considerably strong impact politically and economically," Morita said, speaking before Mitsuzuka's comments.

Hashimoto's remark, perhaps intended to remind Washington that two-way ties are built on more than just trade numbers, could give U.S. proponents of a tough trade stance towards Tokyo just the leverage needed to back up their views.

"I think he made an enormous diplomatic blunder," said Ron Bevacqua, senior economist at Merrill Lynch Japan. "They're doing what they can to correct the mistake. It might work -- it depends on the mood in the Beltway (Washington)."
